title: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom
author: Traditional Caribbean tale, retold — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
Anansi the spider had a big pot. He said, "I will keep all the wisdom in the world in my pot!" He tied the pot to his belly and climbed a tall tree.

The pot was in front of him. It banged on the tree. Anansi could not climb well. His son watched from below.

"Papa," said his son, "tie the pot on your back! Then you can climb." Anansi felt silly. He was not the only one with wisdom after all. He let the wind take the pot, and wisdom spread to everyone.

questions.explanation: Anansi tries to keep all wisdom for himself, fails, and it spreads to everyone — showing that wisdom cannot belong to just one person.

title: A Trip to the Sea Wall
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
On Sunday, Maria and her family walked along the sea wall in Georgetown. The sea wall keeps the ocean water from flooding the city, because much of Guyana's coast is below sea level.

Maria saw fishermen casting their nets and children flying kites in the breeze. Her little brother bought a coconut water from a vendor. They watched the waves crash against the wall until the sun began to set over the Atlantic Ocean.

title: The Kaieteur Falls
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
Deep in the rainforest of Guyana lies one of the most powerful waterfalls in the world: Kaieteur Falls. Water from the Potaro River drops a single, thundering leap of over 220 metres — nearly five times the height of Niagara Falls.

According to legend, the falls are named after Kaie, a Patamona chief who paddled his canoe over the edge to save his people from an enemy attack, offering himself to the Great Spirit. Today, visitors travel by small plane deep into the interior to see the falls, and golden frogs live in the giant tank bromeliad plants that grow nearby, found nowhere else on Earth.

title: The Mashramani Costume
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
Every February, Devika counted down the days until Mashramani, the festival that celebrates Guyana becoming a republic. This year, she had spent weeks helping her aunt sew a costume covered in sequins the colour of the Guyanese flag: green, gold, red, black and white.

On the morning of the parade, Devika's hands trembled as she fastened the last feather to her headdress. She had never marched before, and the thumping soca music from the speakers outside made her stomach flutter with nerves. When she finally stepped onto Republic Avenue, surrounded by dancers and steel pan bands, her nervousness melted away, replaced by a swelling pride that made her want to dance until sunset.

title: The Arapaima of the Rupununi
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
In the slow-moving rivers of Guyana's Rupununi savannah lives one of the largest freshwater fish on Earth: the arapaima. Fully grown, it can measure nearly three metres long and weigh as much as an adult human. Unlike most fish, the arapaima must surface every ten to twenty minutes to gulp air, since it breathes partly through a lung-like organ as well as its gills.

By the early 2000s, overfishing had pushed arapaima populations dangerously low in many rivers. Local Wapishana and Macushi communities, working with conservationists, established a community-managed fishery: fishing was banned in certain lakes, and villagers themselves monitored the population and guided the small number of tourists who came to see the fish. Within a decade, numbers had climbed back so strongly that the programme is now held up as a model of how local communities can protect the wildlife their livelihoods depend on.

title: The Demerara Harbour Bridge Debate
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
For decades, the Demerara Harbour Bridge — a floating pontoon bridge spanning nearly two kilometres across the Demerara River — was the only road link between Georgetown and much of Guyana's west coast. Drivers grew used to the ritual of the retractors opening to let ships pass, sometimes leaving traffic queued for an hour or more.

When the government announced plans for a new, fixed high-span bridge, opinion was divided. Supporters argued that a modern bridge would finally end the delays and support growing trade and travel between the regions. Critics worried about the cost of such a large project and whether smaller communities along the route would benefit as much as the capital. Engineers, meanwhile, pointed out that the river's soft, silty bed made construction more complex than it might first appear, requiring deep foundations to support the structure's weight. Whatever its outcome, the debate reflected a wider question facing the nation: how to balance ambitious infrastructure with the everyday needs of the communities it is meant to serve.

title: Iggy and the Mango Tree
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
Iggy the iguana loved mangoes more than anything. Every morning, he climbed the big mango tree behind his house to pick the ripest one.

One sunny day, Iggy found five mangoes had fallen to the ground. He tried to carry them all at once — one in his mouth, two under his front legs, and two more balanced on his tail. He took one wobbly step and dropped every single mango.

His friend Coco the parrot watched from a branch above. "Why not share some with your friends?" asked Coco. Iggy thought for a moment, then smiled. He gave two mangoes to Coco, gave one to a hungry agouti passing by, and kept two mangoes for himself.

Now Iggy's paws were free, his tummy was full, and he had two new friends to share his lunch with.

title: Stabroek Market
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
In the middle of Georgetown, Guyana's capital city, stands a famous red building with a tall clock tower: Stabroek Market. It was built over a hundred years ago, and its clock tower can be seen from far away across the city.

Inside the market, hundreds of stalls sell fresh fruit, vegetables, fish, spices and clothes. Vendors call out to shoppers, inviting them to look at their goods. The smell of fresh mangoes, peppers and fish fills the air.

Stabroek Market sits right next to the Demerara River, where boats used to bring goods to sell. Even today, it remains one of the busiest and most important places to shop in Georgetown, visited by both local people and tourists every single day.

title: The Giant Water Lily
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
Floating on the still, dark waters of Guyana's rivers and ponds grows one of the most extraordinary plants in the world: the giant water lily, known scientifically as Victoria amazonica. It is Guyana's national flower, and its enormous circular leaves can grow wider than two metres across.

The underside of each leaf is covered in sharp spines and a network of thick, rib-like veins, which help the leaf stay strong enough to float — and even support the weight of a small child, as long as the weight is spread evenly across the leaf.

The giant water lily's flowers are just as remarkable as its leaves. Each flower opens for only two nights. On the first night, it opens pure white and gives off a strong, sweet scent that attracts beetles to pollinate it. By the second night, the flower has changed colour to a deep pink or purple, and it closes for good soon after, sinking beneath the water.

Because it is found nowhere else quite like this, the giant water lily has become a proud symbol of Guyana, appearing on stamps, artwork and even the country's coat of arms.

title: Bauxite: Guyana's Red Gold
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
Deep beneath the forests of Guyana lies a reddish-brown rock called bauxite — sometimes nicknamed "red gold" because of the vital role it has played in the country's economy for over a century.

Bauxite is the raw material used to make aluminium, the lightweight metal found in everything from drink cans to aeroplanes. To extract it, workers dig deep open pits into the earth, then wash and dry the ore before it is shipped abroad for processing.

The town of Linden, built along the Demerara River, grew up almost entirely around the bauxite industry. For decades, thousands of families depended on bauxite mining for their livelihoods, and the town's schools, hospitals and housing were closely tied to the fortunes of the mines.

In recent years, Guyana's economy has grown to depend on other industries too, particularly oil. Even so, bauxite remains an important part of the country's history and continues to be mined and exported today, a reminder of the industry that helped shape Linden and the wider Guyanese economy.

title: The Cricket Match at Bourda Green
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
Every Saturday, Devon walked past Bourda Green on his way to his grandmother's house, watching older boys play cricket on the worn grass pitch. He always imagined himself out there, bat in hand, facing a fast bowler under the hot afternoon sun.

This Saturday was different. As Devon passed, one of the older boys, Ricky, called out to him. "We're short a player — you want to field?" Devon's heart leapt. He nodded quickly before his nerves could talk him out of it.

Fielding turned out to be harder than it looked from the pavement. The ball came at him low and fast, and twice he fumbled it completely, his cheeks burning with embarrassment as the batsmen ran extra runs. But on the third chance, instinct took over — he dived, caught the ball cleanly, and threw it back to the wicketkeeper in one smooth motion.

"Nice catch!" Ricky shouted, grinning. The other boys clapped him on the back. Devon walked the rest of the way to his grandmother's house that evening with grass stains on his knees and a smile he couldn't wipe off his face, already counting the days until next Saturday.

title: Shell Beach: A Refuge for Sea Turtles
author: Original — KaeLex Academy
bodyText:
Along a remote stretch of Guyana's north-western coastline lies Shell Beach, a place unlike anywhere else in the country. Named for the countless shells that wash up along its shore, this quiet beach is one of the most important sea turtle nesting sites in the entire Caribbean region.

Four different species of sea turtle — including the enormous leatherback, which can weigh as much as a small car — return to Shell Beach every year between roughly March and August to lay their eggs in the warm sand, just as their ancestors have done for generations.

For decades, local communities relied on collecting turtle eggs as a source of food and income, a practice that pushed several turtle populations toward serious decline. Recognising the danger, conservationists began working alongside these same communities, training some residents as rangers who now patrol the beach at night, protect nesting females from disturbance, and record data on nests to track the turtles' recovery.

The partnership has not been without its challenges, since balancing conservation with the needs of local livelihoods requires constant compromise. Even so, Shell Beach stands today as an example of how protecting wildlife and supporting the people who live alongside it can, with care and cooperation, go hand in hand.
